slides.title: Learning Arc
slides.notes: Open with the chapter question rather than a definition. A group action is useful because it separates the moves from the objects being moved. Tell students that every example today asks two tests: what is preserved, and what is sorted into equivalent pieces.

slides.title: What Is A Group Action
slides.notes: Make the two axioms feel operational. The identity move must do nothing, and doing one move after another must agree with the group multiplication. The diagram is intentionally simple: it distinguishes the abstract group elements from the visible points that receive their motion.

slides.title: Orbits And Stabilizers
slides.notes: This slide introduces the two bookkeeping devices that drive the chapter. Orbits answer where an object can go, while stabilizers answer which moves are invisible at that object. Stress that both depend on the chosen action, not only on the group.

slides.title: Notebook Certificate
slides.notes: Use the two notebook figures as evidence for the formula rather than as decoration. Six visible tile placements come from a twelve element symmetry group because two moves keep the marked tile fixed. The product is the invariant check students should remember.

slides.title: Faithful And Transitive
slides.notes: Separate two adjectives that students often merge. Faithful means no nontrivial group element acts invisibly on every point. Transitive means the action has one orbit. A single action can have either property, both properties, or neither, depending on the set being acted on.

slides.title: Tilings As Actions
slides.notes: Move from finite examples to geometry in the plane. A tiling is not only a pattern of shapes; it is a set on which a symmetry group acts. The fundamental tile is a representative, and nearby copies are its orbit under allowed motions.

slides.title: Crystallographic Groups
slides.notes: Explain crystallographic groups as controlled infinite symmetry. Translations form the lattice backbone, while finite stabilizers record rotations or reflections that keep a local feature in place. The quotient cell is the compact ledger that makes an infinite pattern countable.

slides.title: Sphere Tilings And Solids
slides.notes: On the sphere, finite rotation groups become especially visible. The same action can be read on vertices, edges, faces, or flags of a solid. Ask students to predict which stabilizer changes when the acted-on set changes while the rotation group stays fixed.

slides.title: Counting By Fixed Points
slides.notes: Burnside style counting is a natural application of the chapter even when the notebook uses the simpler orbit stabilizer certificate. The visible message is that orbits can be counted by averaging fixed data over the group, so symmetry turns enumeration into bookkeeping.

slides.title: Invariant Checklist
slides.notes: Tie the examples back to the notebook's inspection habit. Raw coordinates, colors, and positions usually change, but incidence, distance, orientation, adjacency, or combinatorial type may survive. The correct invariant depends on both the object and the action chosen.

slides.title: Common Pitfalls
slides.notes: Use this as a diagnostic pause. Many wrong solutions come from treating the group as the orbit, assuming stabilizers are always trivial, or proving a fact about the drawing rather than the action. Each warning has a repair question attached.

slides.title: Recap Exercise
slides.notes: Close by having students recompute the chapter's core certificate in a small variation. If the tile had no extra symmetry, the stabilizer would shrink and the orbit would grow. The final takeaway is the reusable equation linking group size, orbit size, and stabilizer size.
